title: Knowing the Book, Missing the King
excerpt: The chief priests knew where the King would be born and never went. How to know the Bible well without missing the One it all points to.

blocks.text: When wise men from the East showed up in Jerusalem asking where the newborn King of the Jews could be found, King Herod panicked. He called in the chief priests and the teachers of the law and asked them where the Messiah was supposed to be born.
They answered at once. Bethlehem, they said, and they quoted the prophet Micah to prove it (Matthew 2:4–6). No hesitation, no looking it up. They knew their Bible cold.
Bethlehem was a short walk from where they were standing. And not one of them went.

Foreign stargazers traveled hundreds of miles for a child they'd only heard about. The men who could recite exactly where to find Him stayed home. It's one of the most unsettling details in the Gospels, and it's easy to read right past it, because we assume that's a story about *them.*
The Warning Jesus Gave
Jesus said something to a group of religious leaders that I think about more than almost anything else He said:

verses: You study the Scriptures diligently because you think that in them you have eternal life. These are the very Scriptures that testify about me, yet you refuse to come to me to have life.

blocks.text: Read it twice. These were people who studied the Bible harder than most of us ever will. Jesus doesn't say they were studying the wrong book. He says the book they loved was pointing straight at Him, and they walked right past the One it pointed to.
It is possible to know a great deal of Scripture and miss Jesus entirely. That's an uncomfortable sentence for anyone who takes the Bible seriously, which is exactly why it needs saying.
How It Happens Quietly
Nobody sets out to do this. It creeps in through habits that look completely respectable.

Some of us read the Bible to win. We go looking for the verse that will settle the next argument, whether that's with a friend, a relative, or a stranger on the internet. Scripture becomes ammunition, and the person across from us becomes an opponent instead of someone loved by God.

Some of us read it as a manual. A tidy guide to a better marriage, a calmer mind, a more organized life. Those things may even be in there, but if that's all we're hunting for, the Bible gets shrunk into a self-improvement book with better credentials.

Some of us read it to defend our system. We've settled on a way of understanding theology, and we're loyal to it, so every passage gets sorted into the right box. The Bible stops being a window and becomes a filing cabinet.

And some of us just collect. Facts, cross-references, the order of the kings, the meaning of the Greek. None of that is bad. Paul warned that "knowledge puffs up while love builds up" (1 Corinthians 8:1), and the puffing can happen so slowly we mistake it for maturity.
Doctrine matters. Careful study matters. But all of it is meant to serve a purpose, and when it stops doing that, we've drifted.
One Story, One Face

Here is what changes how you read everything. On the evening of the first Easter, two disciples were walking to a village called Emmaus, deflated and confused about the events of the past few days. A stranger joined them, listened, and then did something remarkable. "Beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he explained to them what was said in all the Scriptures concerning himself" (Luke 24:27).

All the Scriptures. He didn't pick a few messianic verses. He walked them through the whole thing and showed them Himself in it. Later they said to each other, "Were not our hearts burning within us while he talked with us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?" (24:32).
That is the key. The Bible isn't a collection of unrelated lessons. It's one long story with one central figure.

The Old Testament builds a hope. A promised offspring who would crush the serpent (Genesis 3:15). A lamb provided on a mountain when a father's own son was spared (Genesis 22). A Passover lamb whose blood marked the doors. A suffering servant pierced for our transgressions (Isaiah 53). The Gospels show that hope arriving in flesh. Acts shows Him still at work through His Spirit. The letters explain who He is and what He did. Revelation shows Him finally on the throne, the Lamb who was slain, receiving the worship of all creation.

It looks ahead to Him, it looks back at Him, and then it looks ahead to Him again. That's the shape of the whole book. Paul says "the promises God has made" all find their "Yes" in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20). Every road in Scripture, followed far enough, ends at Him.
The Announcement
If Jesus is the center, then it matters a great deal to be clear about what the good news actually is. It's easy to turn it into something vaguer than it is.

The gospel isn't advice. It's an announcement, the kind a herald makes in the street. Something has happened. Jesus, God's Son, lived the life we were supposed to live and never did. He died on a cross in our place, taking the punishment our sin deserved. He rose from the dead, and in doing so began something new that won't ever end. And now He reigns as King.

Paul called this "of first importance," and he noted twice in two verses that all of it happened "according to the Scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). The Bible and the gospel aren't two separate topics. The Bible is the long road leading to the announcement.

Notice the difference between advice and news. Advice says, *here's what you should do.* News says, *here's what has been done.* One leaves you anxious about whether you'll measure up. The other gives you something to stand on.

But news also demands a response. When Jesus began His ministry, He said, "Repent and believe the good news!" (Mark 1:15). Repent means turning away from our sin and our self-run lives. Believe means trusting and having Faith in Christ alone, not our record, to make us right with God. Repentance and Faith. It isn't one step on a long list. It's the door.
Not Just the Door

Here is where a lot of us get it half right. We believe the gospel is what saves us, and it is. "The gospel... is the power of God that brings salvation to everyone who believes" (Romans 1:16). But then we treat it as the entrance, a thing to get through before we move on to the real work of the Christian life.

Paul pushes back on that. He asks the Galatians, "Are you so foolish? After beginning by means of the Spirit, are you now trying to finish by means of the flesh?" (Galatians 3:3). In other words: you started with grace, so why are you trying to finish on effort?

The same news that saves us also changes us. "The grace of God... teaches us to say 'No' to ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright and godly lives" (Titus 2:11–12). Grace isn't a lenient permission slip. It's a teacher. We don't grow by leaving the gospel behind. We grow by seeing more of it.

And it sends us out. "For Christ's love compels us" (2 Corinthians 5:14). When we're pushed into evangelism by guilt, it tends to be short-lived and joyless. When we're moved by what He has done for us, we can't help but want others to know.
Salvation, growth, and mission all run on the same fuel. We never graduate past the good news. We just keep going deeper into it.
What This Does to Your Bible Reading
So what does this look like on an ordinary Tuesday morning with a cup of coffee and an open Bible?
Maybe just one change. Alongside the usual questions, *what does this say, what should I do*, add another: **what does this show me about Jesus?**

Sometimes the answer is obvious, like in the Gospels. Other times you have to look harder. A story about a flawed king may show your need for a better one. A law you struggle to keep may expose why you needed Someone to keep it for you. A promise that seems too good to be true may turn out to be "Yes" in Him. Even a book like Proverbs, with all its practical wisdom, points to the One Paul calls "the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24).

And here's a quiet test for yourself. After you've read, or after a long theological conversation, where does it leave you? Sharper in an argument? Better informed? More put together? Or more amazed at Christ? The goal of knowing the Scriptures isn't a better résumé. Paul had a remarkable one, and he threw it aside, counting everything a loss "because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord" (Philippians 3:8).
Back to Bethlehem
The chief priests knew where to find the King and stayed put. Maybe the real question for the rest of us isn't how much we know, but whether, when we close the book, we've gone toward Him.
You don't need to know more than you do right now to come to Jesus. And if you already know a lot, you're not too far in to go back to the beginning and look again at who all of it is about.
He's still the One the whole book is pointing to. Everything else is road.

items: How do you usually approach your Bible reading? As ammunition, a manual, a system to defend, or a place to meet Jesus? What would shift if you ended each reading by asking, "What did I see of Him today?"
Do you tend to treat the gospel as the door you walked through or as the ground you still stand on? Where in your life are you trying to "finish by effort" something that began by grace?

If knowing the Bible well hasn't made you more amazed at Jesus, what might be getting in the way? What is one practical step, a slower pace, a passage read aloud, a conversation with another believer, that could help you look for Him again?

blocks.text: Lord Jesus, forgive me for the times I've gone to Your Word looking for everything except You. Open the Scriptures to me the way You did on the road to Emmaus. Let my heart burn again. Keep me from using what I know to puff myself up or to win arguments, and make me someone who is simply more amazed at You. Thank You for the good news, that You lived, died, and rose for me, and that You reign. I repent and trust You alone. Amen.
